## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tuṇḍilajātaka* (Ja 388) is a birth story preserved in the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the discourse is delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk who lived in intense fear of death (*maraṇabhīruko*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. 

In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a boar named Mahātuṇḍila, living with his younger brother Cullatuṇḍila [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. When Cullatuṇḍila is about to be slaughtered by thirty men, he flees to his elder brother, quaking in terror [Cowell 1897]. Mahātuṇḍila comforts him and delivers two verses expounding the Dhamma: because they have been fattened for their meat, escape is impossible; instead, Cullatuṇḍila should plunge into the spotless pool to wash away all stains and obtain an unwaning fragrance [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the closing identification (*samodhāna*), the fearful monk is identified as Cullatuṇḍila, Ānanda as the king, the gathered assembly as the Buddha's assembly, and Mahātuṇḍila as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883]. The *Dhammapada* commentary also references this sermon, noting that thirty companions were swiftly converted and attained arahantship because in this previous life they had observed the five precepts after hearing Mahātuṇḍila's preaching [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b; Weragoda Sarada 1993].

*Parallels and text reuse*: SuttaCentral lists no independent early canonical parallels [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reports eight matching segments of Pali-internal text reuse (totaling 868 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest §1.4–3.4 matching §2550_2–2556) [DharmaNexus]. Across corpora, DharmaNexus detects low-scoring automated textual alignments with the Tibetan version of the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155-2) [DharmaNexus].
